title: Challenge: Rolling-State DP

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only rolling-dp program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Each transition depends only on the previous two states. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `cost=[1,2]`, the worked program returns `1`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `cost=[10,15,20]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Return the minimum cost to move beyond the final stair.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Return the minimum cost to move beyond the final stair. On input `cost=[10,15,20]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Discard table entries once no future transition can read them. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A one-dimensional DP state summarizes a prefix or a single parameter. Define its meaning before writing a recurrence. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n) time · O(1) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test the base state, the first transition, impossible states, and whether an in-place update accidentally reuses an item twice. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `0`. Each transition depends only on the previous two states. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: For costs [10,15,20], costs to land on each stair are 10,15,30. Moving beyond the last stair costs min(15,30)=15. You may start at stair 0 or 1; the final answer is not necessarily the cost at the last stair.
